title: Architecture
text:
Volume ─▶ Lakebase ─▶ bronze ─▶ silver ─▶ model ─▶ gold ─▶ Lakebase ─▶ CRM
  CSV      Postgres      Delta     Delta            Delta   reverse ETL
                                                        └─▶ parquet ─▶ public app
Lakebase is Postgres 17 running inside Databricks: the operational side. Single rows, foreign keys, low latency. It is where the retention team’s system reads.
Delta under Unity Catalog is the analytical side. Columns, history, large scans, time travel.
They are two engines because they solve two different problems. There is also an operational reason: an analytical scan over the transactional database would compete with the writes of the system that actually depends on it.

The predictions travel back to Postgres. A model whose output never reaches the system that makes the decision has not finished.

title: Architecture
section: The medallion layers, and the rule each one keeps
text:
The medallion layers, and the rule each one keeps








Layer
What lives there
The rule




bronze
The source file, unchanged
Nothing is corrected here. Fidelity beats cleanliness


silver
Typed, clean, four derived features
Only deterministic features — nothing that learns a statistic


gold
Predictions and tables the app reads
One writer per table, no exceptions



That middle rule is the anti-leakage control. Anything that learns from data — scaling, encoding, imputation — lives inside the scikit-learn Pipeline, which is fitted after the train/test split and inside each cross-validation fold. A scaler fitted in silver would have seen the test rows, and every number reported afterwards would be quietly optimistic.

title: Architecture
text:
Privacy enforced by the schema
surname exists in the landing table, because that table is a faithful copy of the source. It does not exist in the modelled table.
The constraint is imposed by the schema rather than by the discipline of whoever writes the next query. A column that does not exist cannot be leaked by accident, and the boundary holds all the way to the operational query the CRM runs.

title: Architecture
text:
The reverse ETL








Figure 1: The 800 contacts are not split evenly. Each country receives a share proportional to its expected churners, which is why Germany takes roughly the same quota as France with half the customers.





The write back to Lakebase is append-only: one row per customer per scoring run. That way what was predicted at a given moment can be reconstructed, instead of overwriting the past. Both writes are idempotent — the run is upserted and the predictions are deleted for that run before reloading — so running the cell twice leaves the same state as running it once.

title: Bank Customer Churn
text: 10,000 customers · 20.4% annual churn · 800 calls per campaign · Databricks

title: Bank Customer Churn
text:
The question
A bank loses one customer in five every year and has budget to call 800 of them before they go. The question is not who will leave — nobody decides that. It is who to call with the calls you have.
That constraint changes the problem. Recovering a customer is worth 145 €; bothering one who was staying costs 35 €. From those two numbers a threshold falls out:
\[p^* = \frac{35}{145 + 35} = 0.194\]
Below that probability, calling destroys value. But with fixed capacity the threshold that actually applies is not the profitable one — it is the one the quota imposes. The 800 highest-risk customers go in, and the cut lands at 0.73.
Capacity turns classification into ranking. Everything else on this site follows from that sentence: the metric, the rival to beat, and the ceiling the project could not cross.

The model is not judged against random guessing. It is judged against the rule the bank could apply tomorrow with no model at all.

title: Bank Customer Churn
text:
How it was built
Eight notebooks running from a local machine against Databricks through Databricks Connect: Lakebase (Postgres 17) for the operational side, Unity Catalog and Delta for the analytical side, MLflow for tracking and the model registry, and a Streamlit dashboard for the retention team.

The dataset is synthetic, and the project proves it rather than assuming it — four independent signs, none of them looked for on purpose. That places a ceiling on what any model can learn here, and the ceiling is stated instead of hidden.

What it is for
The campaigns team does not need a metrics report. They need a list of customers with an action attached, and a reason to trust the number next to each name.
The dashboard has five sections: an executive summary with the calibration check in plain sight, segmentation with filters, the ranked list with a suggested action, model performance, and an individual scorer.

The reason for the split is practical. A free-tier SQL warehouse stops itself after inactivity, and pointing a public app at it would mean either publishing credentials to a third-party service or leaving the page unreachable most of the time.

A dashboard showing ten thousand pre-scored rows does not need a query engine behind it. The pipeline is what demonstrates the Databricks work — the dashboard is a presentation layer, and treating it as one is what makes it openable by anyone.

section: The scorer is a test, not a toy
text:
The scorer is a test, not a toy
The individual prediction section carries a field guide and eight preset profiles. Each profile states the risk level the analysis leads you to expect before you score it, and the result reports whether the model agreed.
Four of the nine fields should barely move the prediction. credit_score from 350 to 850, estimated_salary from 12 to 199,000 — the probability hardly shifts. That is not a defect: those variables have no signal, and that was established separately before anything was trained.

Intuition says older means riskier. The data says active customers over 60 churn less than a forty-year-old. If both profiles come out similar, the model did not capture the age × activity interaction and something is wrong upstream — which is exactly what a demonstration is for.

title: Findings
text:
The three strongest relationships in this dataset are non-monotonic, and in all three the correlation coefficient misleads.
num_of_products spans 92 points between groups — from 7.6% churn at two products to 100% at four — and its Spearman correlation with churn is −0.05. A feature selection step filtering on |ρ| > 0.1 would have deleted the strongest predictor in the table.
The reason is mechanical. Correlation measures monotonicity. Risk falls from one product to two and then explodes at three and four; averaged over the range, the ups cancel the downs.

This is already an argument about model choice, made before any model existed. A linear model has to be told about a shape like this. A tree finds it alone.

title: Findings
section: The finding that changed the conclusion
text:
The finding that changed the conclusion
Exploration first established that age describes an inverted U: risk climbs to the 50-59 band and falls after. That turned out to be a composition artefact.








Figure 1: Split by activity, the inverted U disappears. Among inactive customers risk never stops climbing; among active ones it does fall after 60. The aggregate curve only bends because the share of active customers changes across age bands.





Two consequences follow, and both are decisions rather than observations.
On modelling. A model that treats age additively cannot represent this. It has to capture an interaction — an argument for trees over linear models, made from the data rather than from preference.
On the business. The highest-risk cell in the whole dataset is inactive and over 60. And activity is the one variable the bank can actually change. Age is observed; inactivity is fought.

title: Findings
section: The confounder that halved an effect
text:
The confounder that halved an effect
Customers with zero balance churn at 13.8% against 24.1% for those with a balance — a gap of 10.3 points, and it looks conclusive.
Except Germany has not one single customer with zero balance, and Germany churns at 32.4%. Every German sits in the “has a balance” bucket, dragging it up.
Removing Germany, the gap falls to 4.9 points. The effect is real and half the size it looked. Reporting the 10.3 would not have been a lie, but it would have been wrong — and nobody would have caught it without the country breakdown.

title: Findings
section: Four signs the data is synthetic
text:
Four signs the data is synthetic
None of these was looked for. All four turned up pulling on a quality check.









Signal
Why it gives the game away




1
Salary with skew 0.00 and kurtosis −1.18
The exact values of a uniform distribution. Real salaries pile up low with a long right tail


2
Age and tenure correlate at −0.01
In real data tenure grows with age. These were drawn independently


3
All 60 customers with four products left
100% across sixty cases is a rule, not a behaviour


4
No outlier possible in salary
In a uniform distribution the interquartile fences fall outside the data by construction



The second explains the 322 accounts apparently opened before the customer turned 18. There are no corrupt rows to clean: the generator rolled one die for age and another for tenure, and some combinations came out impossible.

The honest implication. The interactions a model can learn here are limited to the ones the generator introduced. Detecting that from the internal inconsistencies is worth more than repeating that it is “a clean dataset of ten thousand rows with no nulls”.

title: Findings
section: Two effects with no available explanation
text:
Two effects with no available explanation
Germany churns at twice the rate of France and Spain while being indistinguishable on every observable variable — same mean age, same share of active customers, same product counts. Women churn at 25.1% against 16.5% for men, and the gap replicates inside all three countries.
Both variables predict well precisely because they stand in for something not measured. That is what makes them dangerous rather than useful, and it is why the deployed model does not use gender.

title: The Model
section: Why KNN and SVM were never tried
text:
Why KNN and SVM were never tried
KNN classifies by proximity, and proximity has no meaning across these columns. It would mix euros of balance, years of age and a country into a single distance. That can be normalised, but the resulting number corresponds to nothing.
SVM has a more concrete problem: it does not produce probabilities natively. It returns a side of a boundary. This system does not need a yes or no — it needs to rank the portfolio to allocate 800 calls. Without probability there is no ranking.

Neither was rejected on performance. They were rejected because they do not fit the shape of the decision, and testing a model you could not use even if it won is time spent on nothing.

title: The Model
text:
What the model uses








Figure 2: Permutation importance measured on unseen data. In grey, variables whose effect is smaller than their own error — indistinguishable from zero, so the ordering among them is not interpretable.





Permutation importance rather than the forest’s built-in impurity measure, which favours variables with many distinct values regardless of signal. It has two traps, and both were hit at least once during the work: measuring columns the pipeline discards, which produces phantom zeros that push real variables down the table; and measuring on training data, where importance reflects what the model memorised rather than what helps it predict.

title: The Model
text:
Calibration is not cosmetic
The forest was trained with class_weight="balanced_subsample", which improves ranking and inflates the probabilities.
For ranking that is harmless. But this system compares against a break-even threshold of 0.194 that came out of the cost model. If the probability is not a probability, that threshold means nothing.








Figure 3: Mean predicted probability against observed churn, per risk level. The two bars tracking each other is the proof. Isotonic calibration learns a monotonic function, so it corrects the scale without being able to damage the ranking.

title: The Model
section: The two criteria that were not met
text:
The two criteria that were not met
Eight criteria were registered before any model was trained. Six were met. The two that failed are reported as failures, and neither was adjusted afterwards.

The country recall gap
A gap of 20.1 points against a 10-point criterion. It is not a bug: it is the consequence of one global threshold applied to groups with different base rates. Germany churns at twice the rate, so it absorbs a larger share of the quota.
Equalising it is possible and it was priced: roughly 720 € per campaign in lost value. Equalising recall across groups with different base rates is mathematically incompatible with holding other desirable properties at once. This project does not promise a fair system — it measures the gap, prices it, and leaves the decision with the business.


The recall criterion was impossible








Figure 4: With fixed capacity, no model can exceed the ratio of contacts to churners. The criterion asked for 0.60; the arithmetic allows 0.393.







criterion       : 0.60
reachable ceiling: 0.3931   (a perfect oracle)
model reached    : 0.3489   = 88.8% of the maximum


The criterion was not lowered so it could pass. It stayed where it was, it failed, and the reason it was impossible is explained. Moving the target after seeing the result is the one thing that cannot be defended.
